name: Letter position shift
statement: \text{code}_i = \text{word}_i + d_i \pmod{26},\ d_i \text{ constant, alternating } (+a, -a) \text{ or increasing } (+1, +2, +3, \dots)
derivation: Line up word and code letter by letter.
Find each $d_i$ from alphabet positions (A=1, ..., Z=26), wrapping Z $\to$ A.
Name the pattern: constant, alternating or increasing.
Check it on the second word, then apply it to the asked word.
No pattern: try [[f:coding.reverse-then-shift]] or [[f:coding.vowel-consonant-shift]].
shortcut: Check the first two letters of every option against the first two shifted letters; usually only one option survives.

steps: RIVAL $\to$ PKTCJ: R$-2$, I$+2$, V$-2$, A$+2$, L$-2$ (alternating).
POINT: N, Q, G, P, R $\to$ NQGPR, answer (C).

common_traps: Reading the shift backwards (code to word), which gives the decoded word instead of the code.
Losing the alternation when the target is longer or shorter than the example word.
Stopping after two letters: RIVAL starts $-2, +2$ but every letter must be checked.

name: Reverse then shift
statement: \text{code} = \text{shift}(\text{reverse}(\text{word})):\ \text{if no direct shift fits, reverse the word and find the shifts again}
derivation: Clue: the code's first letter is close to the word's last letter.
Write the word backwards.
Find the per-letter shifts between the reversed word and the code, as in [[f:coding.letter-position-shift]].
Confirm on the second word, then reverse the asked word and apply the shifts.

steps: NAME reversed = EMAN; $+1$ each gives FNBO.
NAIL reversed = LIAN; $+1$ gives MJBO, answer (D).

common_traps: Shifting before reversing: with alternating shifts BLEW gives VFKC instead of XDMA; reverse first.
Shifting the original word: NAIL $+1$ gives OBJM, which is not even an option.
Picking the option with the right letters in the wrong order (MJOB instead of MJBO).

verification.code:
P = lambda ch: ord(ch) - 64
L = lambda p: chr((p - 1) % 26 + 65)

def shifts(w, c):
    return [((P(b) - P(a) + 13) % 26) - 13 for a, b in zip(w, c)]

def infer(d):
    if len(set(d)) == 1:
        return lambda i: d[0]
    if len(d) > 2 and all(d[i] == d[i % 2] for i in range(len(d))):
        return lambda i: d[i % 2]
    s = d[1] - d[0]
    if all(d[i + 1] - d[i] == s for i in range(len(d) - 1)):
        return lambda i: d[0] + s * i
    return None

def apply(rule, w):
    return "".join(L(P(ch) + rule(i)) for i, ch in enumerate(w))

def learn(examples):
    rule = infer(shifts(*examples[0]))
    if rule is None or any(apply(rule, w) != c for w, c in examples):
        return None
    return rule

def code(examples, target, options):
    direct = learn(examples)
    rev = learn([(w[::-1], c) for w, c in examples])
    rule, word = (direct, target) if direct else (rev, target[::-1])
    assert rule is not None
    return direct is None, [lab for lab, v in options.items() if v == apply(rule, word)]

# worked example 2024-09-09_0900_R05: NAME -> FNBO, NANO -> POBO, NAIL -> ?
assert code([("NAME", "FNBO"), ("NANO", "POBO")], "NAIL",
            {"A": "MOBJ", "B": "MJOB", "C": "MOJB", "D": "MJBO"}) == (True, ["D"])
# 2024-09-25_1600_R12: CASE -> FTBD, CAKE -> FLBD, CALF -> ?
assert code([("CASE", "FTBD"), ("CAKE", "FLBD")], "CALF",
            {"A": "GBDM", "B": "GBMD", "C": "GMBD", "D": "GMDB"}) == (True, ["C"])
# 2024-09-10_0900_R04: reverse, then +1/-1 alternately
assert code([("BELL", "MKFA"), ("BOND", "EMPA")], "BLEW",
            {"A": "XDMA", "B": "XMDA", "C": "XMAD", "D": "XDAM"}) == (True, ["A"])
# constructed control: a plain +2 shift is found directly, no reversal needed
assert code([("PEN", "RGP"), ("CUP", "EWR")], "BOX", {"A": "DQZ", "B": "ZQD", "C": "DQY", "D": "CPY"}) == (False, ["A"])

name: Vowel/consonant rule
statement: \text{code}_i = \text{word}_i + d_v \text{ if vowel (A, E, I, O, U)},\ \text{word}_i + d_c \text{ if consonant},\ d_v \neq d_c \text{ (often } d_v = 0\text{)}
derivation: Clue: vowels in the word stay vowels or neighbours in the code, while consonants move by a fixed step.
Mark the vowels in the example word.
Find the shift for vowels $d_v$ and for consonants $d_c$ separately; each must be constant.
Confirm on the second example, then code the asked word letter by letter by type.

steps: SILK $\to$ TIML: S$+1$, I stays, L$+1$, K$+1$.
CHANGE: C$\to$D, H$\to$I, A, N$\to$O, G$\to$H, E $\to$ DIAOHE, answer (C).

common_traps: Shifting vowels with the consonant step: CHANGE becomes DIBOHF, not an option.
Treating Y as a vowel; in these questions only A, E, I, O, U are vowels.
Deciding the type after shifting instead of from the original letter.

name: Letter rearrangement
statement: \text{code} = \text{word with its letters reordered by a fixed position map (reverse, reverse all but last, halves swapped, pairs swapped)}
derivation: Clue: code and word have exactly the same letters.
Number the word's positions 1 to n and write under each code letter the position it came from.
Read the map (e.g. 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 8 = first seven reversed, last kept).
Check it on the second word, then move the asked word's letters the same way.

steps: RETAINE|D $\to$ ENIATER|D: first seven letters reversed, last kept.

common_traps: Reversing the whole word when the last letter stays fixed (FIREWALL reversed is LLAWERIF, not LAWERIFL).
Mapping by letter instead of by position when a letter repeats.
Choosing an option that has the right letters but one swapped pair.

verification.code:
from itertools import permutations

def perms(examples):
    n = len(examples[0][0])
    assert all(len(w) == len(c) == n and sorted(w) == sorted(c) for w, c in examples)
    return [p for p in permutations(range(n))
            if all("".join(w[i] for i in p) == c for w, c in examples)]

def code(examples, target, options):
    ps = perms(examples)
    outs = {"".join(target[i] for i in p) for p in ps}
    assert len(outs) == 1
    out = outs.pop()
    return ps[0], [lab for lab, v in options.items() if v == out]

# worked example 2024-09-13_1230_R07: reverse first seven letters, keep the last
p, ans = code([("RETAINED", "ENIATERD"), ("MATURITY", "TIRUTAMY")], "FIREWALL",
              {"A": "LAWEFIFR", "B": "FLIREWAL", "C": "LAWERIFL", "D": "FLLAWERI"})
assert p == (6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 7) and ans == ["C"]
# 2024-09-17_0900_R09: same rule
assert code([("BIRTHDAY", "ADHTRIBY"), ("CONGRESS", "SERGNOCS")], "DIVISION",
            {"A": "NDOISIVI", "B": "DNOISIVI", "C": "OISIVIDN", "D": "NOISIVID"})[1] == ["C"]
# constructed: halves swapped
assert code([("CODE", "DECO"), ("WORK", "RKWO")], "LAMP",
            {"A": "MPLA", "B": "PMAL", "C": "LAMP", "D": "AMPL"})[1] == ["A"]

name: Common element elimination
statement: \text{word in sentences } S_1 \text{ and } S_2 \Rightarrow \text{its code is in } \text{codes}(S_1) \cap \text{codes}(S_2);\ \text{remove codes of sentences without it}
derivation: Word order and code order are unrelated; work with sets.
For the asked word, intersect the code sets of every sentence that contains it.
Remove every code that belongs to a sentence without the word.
One code left: that is the answer. Two left: the code cannot be determined.

steps: 'where' is in sentences 1 and 2: $\{aa, dd, ff\} \cap \{dd, zz, pp\} = \{dd\}$.
'what' is in sentences 1 and 3: $\{aa, dd, ff\} \cap \{ff, kk, ll\} = \{ff\}$.
'how' gets the code left in sentence 1: aa, answer (A).

common_traps: Matching by position: 'how' is the third word but 'ff' (third code) belongs to 'what'.
Forgetting the third sentence, which leaves two codes for the word.
Answering a code for a word that appears in only one sentence when that sentence has other unknown words.

verification.code:
def decode(sentences, word):
    # candidates = codes of every sentence with the word, minus codes of every sentence without it
    cand = None
    for words, codes in sentences:
        if word in words:
            cand = set(codes) if cand is None else cand & set(codes)
    for words, codes in sentences:
        if word not in words:
            cand -= set(codes)
    return cand

def answer(sentences, word, options):
    cand = decode(sentences, word)
    assert len(cand) == 1
    return [lab for lab, v in options.items() if v in cand]

S1 = [("what where how".split(), "aa dd ff".split()),
      ("where there that".split(), "dd zz pp".split()),
      ("which what here".split(), "ff kk ll".split())]
# worked example 2024-09-09_0900_R20
assert decode(S1, "where") == {"dd"} and decode(S1, "what") == {"ff"}
assert answer(S1, "how", {"A": "aa", "B": "kk", "C": "zz", "D": "ff"}) == ["A"]
# 2024-09-09_1230_R06
S2 = [("let it go".split(), "vc nt ap".split()), ("this is it".split(), "mq vc lh".split())]
assert answer(S2, "it", {"A": "nt", "B": "lh", "C": "vc", "D": "mq"}) == ["C"]
# 2024-09-09_1230_R11
S3 = [("It's your life".split(), "Ao Bo Co".split()), ("It's your food".split(), "Ba Co Bo".split())]
assert answer(S3, "food", {"A": "Ba", "B": "Bo", "C": "Ao", "D": "Co"}) == ["A"]
# with only two sentences, 'let' cannot be fixed: two codes remain
assert decode(S2, "let") == {"nt", "ap"}

name: Letter position values
statement: \text{each letter} \to p \text{ (A=1, ..., Z=26) or } 27 - p \text{ (Z=1, ..., A=26)}, \text{ possibly } \pm c;\ \text{write the numbers side by side}
derivation: Split the code into numbers that match the word's letters (1 or 2 digits each).
Compare the first letter's number with $p$ and with $27 - p$.
The gap from the closer one is the constant $c$; check it on every letter.
Code the asked word letter by letter and join the numbers in order.
common_traps: Splitting the digit string wrongly: G = 22 and L = 17, not 2, 21, 71.
Using $27 - p$ when the constant is $+2$, which gives $27 - 9 = 18$ for I instead of 20 (option B pattern).
Joining the numbers in reverse order.

verification.code:
P = lambda ch: ord(ch) - 64

def rules(examples):
    out = []
    for name, f in (("p", P), ("27-p", lambda ch: 27 - P(ch))):
        for c in range(-26, 27):
            g = lambda ch, f=f, c=c: f(ch) + c
            if all("".join(str(g(ch)) for ch in w) == code for w, code in examples):
                out.append((name, c, g))
    return out

def answer(examples, target, options):
    rs = rules(examples)
    assert len(rs) == 1
    out = "".join(str(rs[0][2](ch)) for ch in target)
    return rs[0][:2], [lab for lab, v in options.items() if v == out]

# worked example 2024-09-13_1230_R01: code = (27 - p) + 2 = 29 - p
assert answer([("GLOBAL", "221714272817"), ("FOREST", "23141124109")], "IMPACT",
              {"A": "20161328269", "B": "18141126247", "C": "20161226259", "D": "20161327259"}) == (("27-p", 2), ["A"])
# constructed: plain positions p
assert answer([("CAB", "312"), ("HEN", "8514")], "DOG",
              {"A": "4157", "B": "4158", "C": "41520", "D": "3157"}) == (("p", 0), ["A"])

name: Sum/count of letter values
statement: \text{code} = f(S, n),\ S = \textstyle\sum p \text{ (or } \sum (27-p)\text{)},\ n = \text{number of letters};\ \text{test } S,\ S \pm k,\ S \cdot n,\ n \cdot k
derivation: Compute $S$ with $p$ (A=1) and with $27 - p$ (Z=1) for the first word.
Compare with the code: equal, off by a constant, or a multiple of $S$ or of $n$.
If the code is divisible by $n$, check $\text{code} \div n$ against $S$.
Keep only the rule that also fits the second word, then apply it.
common_traps: Stopping at the forward sum: HIT forward is 37 and 132 is not a multiple of 37.
Ignoring $n$: 132 and 144 come from different-length words, so try dividing by 3 and 4.
Missing a pure count rule (BLEACHERS 9 letters $	imes 7 = 63$) while adding letter values.

verification.code:
from fractions import Fraction as F
P = lambda ch: ord(ch) - 64
VALUES = {"p": P, "27-p": lambda ch: 27 - P(ch)}

def rules(examples):
    out = []
    for vn, v in VALUES.items():
        S = lambda w, v=v: sum(v(ch) for ch in w)
        w0, c0 = examples[0]
        cands = [
            ("S+k", lambda w, k, S=S: S(w) + k, c0 - S(w0)),
            ("S*k", lambda w, k, S=S: S(w) * k, F(c0, S(w0))),
            ("S*n+k", lambda w, k, S=S: S(w) * len(w) + k, c0 - S(w0) * len(w0)),
            ("S+n*k", lambda w, k, S=S: S(w) + len(w) * k, F(c0 - S(w0), len(w0))),
            ("n*k", lambda w, k: len(w) * k, F(c0, len(w0))),
        ]
        for name, f, k in cands:
            if all(f(w, k) == c for w, c in examples):
                out.append((vn, name, k, f))
    return out

def answer(examples, target, options):
    rs = rules(examples)
    assert rs
    preds = {r[3](target, r[2]) for r in rs}
    return [lab for lab, v in options.items() if v in preds]

# worked example 2024-09-18_1230_R08: (sum of 27 - p) x number of letters
rs = rules([("HIT", 132), ("SBYZ", 144)])
assert [(r[0], r[1], r[2]) for r in rs] == [("27-p", "S*n+k", 0)]
assert answer([("HIT", 132), ("SBYZ", 144)], "YRF", {"A": 108, "B": 124, "C": 112, "D": 96}) == ["D"]
# 2024-09-24_1230_R20: plain sum
assert answer([("IFF", 21), ("ARB", 21)], "CAW", {"A": 25, "B": 23, "C": 27, "D": 26}) == ["C"]
# 2024-09-24_1600_R15: number of letters x 7
assert answer([("BLEACHERS", 63), ("ABACAS", 42)], "FIZZY", {"A": 52, "B": 45, "C": 44, "D": 35}) == ["D"]
# 2024-09-13_1600_R22: sum + 10
assert answer([("ESTATE", 80), ("FAMOUS", 85)], "FOREST", {"A": 88, "B": 90, "C": 93, "D": 83}) == ["C"]

name: Reverse alphabet positions
statement: r(\text{letter}) = 27 - p:\ \text{Z}=1, \text{Y}=2, \dots, \text{A}=26;\ \text{used per letter or summed}
derivation: Writing the alphabet backwards puts A at 26 and Z at 1.
A letter at position $p$ is the $(27 - p)$th from Z, because $p + (27 - p) = 27$.
It is the position of the opposite letter [[f:alphabet.opposite-letter]].
Summed form: $\sum (27 - p) = 27n - \sum p$ for an $n$-letter word.
shortcut: Sum of reverse values $= 27n - (\text{forward sum})$: SET $= 81 - 44 = 37$.
common_traps: Using forward positions: SET forward sum is 44, not 37.
Using $26 - p$, which makes Z = 0 and every value one too small.
Mixing forward for one word and reverse for another.

verification.code:
P = lambda ch: ord(ch) - 64
R = lambda ch: 27 - P(ch)
ALPHA = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
assert all(R(ch) == ALPHA[::-1].index(ch) + 1 for ch in ALPHA)   # Z=1 ... A=26

def sum_code(examples, target, options):
    assert any(sum(P(ch) for ch in w) != c for w, c in examples)   # forward sum fails
    assert all(sum(R(ch) for ch in w) == c for w, c in examples)
    return [lab for lab, v in options.items() if v == sum(R(ch) for ch in target)]

def each_code(examples, target, options):
    assert all([R(ch) for ch in w] == c for w, c in examples)
    return [lab for lab, v in options.items() if v == [R(ch) for ch in target]]

# worked example 2024-09-09_1600_R25: SET 37, MIX 35, WAR ?
assert sum_code([("SET", 37), ("MIX", 35)], "WAR", {"A": 29, "B": 39, "C": 21, "D": 32}) == ["B"]
# 2024-09-18_1600_R02: each letter separately
assert each_code([("MORE", [14, 12, 9, 22]), ("KNOW", [16, 13, 12, 4])], "SAID",
                 {"A": [8, 26, 18, 23], "B": [8, 26, 17, 23], "C": [7, 25, 18, 23], "D": [7, 26, 18, 22]}) == ["A"]
